title: Differentiation Rules
body:
The table that replaces the limit definition of the [[Derivative]]. Learn it cold; the rest of the
course assumes you can differentiate anything on sight.

## The algebraic rules

| Rule | Statement |
|---|---|
| constant | $\frac{d}{dx}c = 0$ |
| power | $\frac{d}{dx}x^n = nx^{n-1}$, for **every** real $n$ |
| constant multiple | $(cf)' = cf'$ |
| sum / difference | $(f \pm g)' = f' \pm g'$ |
| **product** | $(fg)' = f'g + fg'$ |
| **quotient** | $\left(\dfrac{f}{g}\right)' = \dfrac{f'g - fg'}{g^2}$ |
| composition | see [[Chain Rule]] |

> **The derivative of a product is not the product of the derivatives.** Same for quotients. Sum
> and difference are the only rules that work the naive way, and the reason people get burned is
> that those two are taught first.

Quotient rule mnemonic: **low d-high minus high d-low, over low squared**. The subtraction does not
commute, so getting the order backwards flips the sign of every answer.

The power rule covers more than it looks like: $\sqrt{x} = x^{1/2}$ differentiates to
$\frac{1}{2}x^{-1/2}$, and $\frac{1}{x^3} = x^{-3}$ to $-3x^{-4}$. Rewrite roots and reciprocals as
exponents *before* differentiating and the quotient rule is rarely needed.

## The transcendentals

| $f(x)$ | $f'(x)$ |
|---|---|
| $e^x$ | $e^x$ |
| $a^x$ | $a^x \ln a$ |
| $\ln x$ | $1/x$ |
| $\log_a x$ | $\dfrac{1}{x \ln a}$ |
| $\sin x$ | $\cos x$ |
| $\cos x$ | $-\sin x$ |
| $\tan x$ | $\sec^2 x$ |
| $\arcsin x$ | $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$ |
| $\arctan x$ | $\dfrac{1}{1+x^2}$ |

$e^x$ is its own derivative, and that is the definition of $e$ rather than a coincidence: $e$ is
the base for which the exponential's growth rate equals its value. See [[Trigonometric Function]]
for the trig half and the period-4 cycle.

Note the pattern in the inverse trig derivatives: they are **algebraic**. Differentiating a trig
function gives trig back, but differentiating its inverse gives you a square root or a rational
function. Run backwards, that is why $\int \frac{dx}{1+x^2}$ has an $\arctan$ in the answer, which
is most of what [[Integration By Trigonometric Substitution]] is doing in [[CALCULUS 2]].

## Worked example

$$
f(x) = x^2 e^x \sin x
$$

Two products, so apply the rule twice (group as $(x^2 e^x)\cdot \sin x$):

```
(x²eˣ)'          = 2x·eˣ + x²·eˣ        product rule
f'(x)            = (2x eˣ + x² eˣ)·sin x + x² eˣ·cos x
                 = x eˣ (2 sin x + x sin x + x cos x)
```

The factoring at the end is not optional busywork: [[Curve Sketching]] and [[Optimization]] both
need $f' = 0$ solved, and an unfactored derivative is not solvable by inspection.
